cards.claim: IFNSO reduces matrix multiplication burden in orthogonalization from N to 1 operation along the long dimension
cards.conditions: Matrix orthogonalization, tested on matrices of sizes 100×100, 1000×1000, 2000×2000
cards.effect: Computational cost reduction: from O(N·m·n²) to O(m·n²) where N is number of iterations
cards.evidence: Experimental comparison in Section 3.4.2 and Table 1 showing FLOPs and error metrics
cards.quote: our method demonstrates competitive efficiency by reducing the number of computationally expensive operations from to , where is more costly than because . This advantage stems from its lower cost of floating-point computations, achieved by reducing the amount of computation along the -axis.

cards.claim: Constrained polynomial coefficients enable stable optimization and faster convergence of learnable coefficients
cards.conditions: Coefficient learning using Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001, step decay, 100 epochs sampling from interval (0,1)
cards.effect: Stable gradient flow during optimization; convergence to 1 as input approaches 1
cards.evidence: Mathematical formulation in Eq. 20-21 and empirical convergence shown in Figures 3 and 7
cards.quote: we impose constraints on the coefficients: where the coefficients are constrained such that as . ... To ensure stable convergence during optimization, we impose constraints on the coefficients

cards.claim: Exponential growth of polynomial exponents provides better approximation coverage than linear growth with same number of terms
cards.conditions: Polynomial term selection strategy for orthogonalization
cards.effect: Exponential growth expands power range faster, enabling broader coverage with fewer terms
cards.evidence: Comparative analysis in Section 2.2 and Figure 2 (linear vs exponential growth visualization)
cards.quote: exponential growth expands the range of powers much faster than linear growth, enabling broader coverage with the same number of terms. Based on this observation, we adopt an exponential growth in parameterization

cards.claim: IFNSO achieves best validation performance compared to other Newton-Schulz variants in short training (≤10 epochs)
cards.conditions: MNIST dataset, Muon optimizer, batch size 32, max 10 epochs, 6:1 train/test split, cross-entropy loss
cards.effect: Loss 4.25 (vs Muon's NS 5.10, Original NS 6.78, Cesista 5.47, CANS 10.62); Accuracy 98.87% (vs Muon 98.83%)
cards.evidence: Table 2 comparative results and Figure 7 training loss curves
cards.quote: Following the experimental setup detailed in Section 3.2.1, we compare our proposed strategy (IFSNO) with existing methods applied to the Muon optimizer for training a simple neural network on the MNIST dataset. As shown in Table 2, the network optimized using our strategy yields the best performance. Correspondingly, Figure 7 demonstrates that the model trained with our NS iteration algorithm achieves the fastest convergence.

cards.claim: Computational burden of IFNSO grows more slowly with matrix size than other Newton-Schulz methods
cards.conditions: Matrix sizes tested: 100×100, 1000×1000, 2000×2000; orthogonalization performance measurement
cards.effect: FLOPs and orthogonalization error remain lower as matrix dimension increases
cards.evidence: Table 1 quantitative comparison of FLOP counts across methods at different matrix sizes
cards.quote: Specifically, as increases, the computational burden of our method grows more slowly compared to other methods. Our method also achieves competitive orthogonalization performance.
